chapter: Early 1930s: Bessie Smith, Rex Stewart and the Harlem scene
title: Why Harlem entertainment declined
summary: Dance theatres, movies and vaudeville flourished then; Ramirez and Dance discuss population, the decline of Harlem venues, and past competitiveness against present mediocrity.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience

blocks.x: What I was really getting at was: Economically, it seems as though the Black people could almost afford entertainment and a good time better then than they can now. Not a lot goes on in Harlem now.

Well, yeah... Well, as I said before... Well, you must realize, in those years there was 150 million people population in the United States. Today it's almost 350 million [SIC: 250 MILLION]. That's a big difference. You have the same mode of government going on. But much less that people are going to have now. If that doesn't grow, that creates difficulties, because everything is jammed up. I mean, sooner or later something has got to happen, because you don't have enough hospitals, you don't have enough judges, you don't have enough jails, you don't have enough of anything! But you've got a lot of people. Do you follow what I'm saying?

Yes. What I am sort of thinking now is when you had all those theatres up there, the Apollo and the Lafayette, and you had these big ballrooms... Of course, that was partly because there were talkies, the movies, but...
The movies, yeah... People went to the movies a good deal more, more than they do today.
I mean, they went to the movies in a big way in the Twenties, didn't they.
Yeah, movies... And believe it or not, they had a lot of Colored movies. But of course, at that time we had also entertainment, we had vaudeville...
Yeah. Well, that's what I'm getting at.
There's been a tremendous change, hasn't there?
I mean, all these places that people played and entertained, they are virtually gone. There's nothing much up there, is there?
I guess there was a struggle for perfection in whatever you did.
